source_text:
Igitur cum omnes hac spectaculi uoluptate caperemur, Caecuius nihil intendere neque de contentione ridere, sed tacens, anxius, segregatus dolere nescio quid uultu fatebatur.
cui ego: Quid hoc est rei? cur non agnosco, Caecili, alacritatem tuam illam?
et illam ocnloram etiam in seriis hilaritatem requiro. tum ille: Iam dudum meOctaui nostri acriter angit et remordet oratio, qua in te inuectus obiurgauit neglegentiae, ut me dissimulanter grauius argueret inscientiae..
itaque progrediar ulterius: de toto et integro mihi cum Octauio res est. si placet, ut ipsius sectae homo cum eo disputem, iam profecto intelleget facilius esse in contubernalibus disputare quam conserere sapientiam:
modo in istis ad tutelam balnearum iactis et in altum procurrentibus petrarum obicibus residamus, ut et requiescere de itinere possimus et intentius disputare.
et cum dicto eius adsedimus, ita ut me ex tribus medium lateris ambitione protegerent: nec hoc obsequi fuit aut ordinis aut honoris, quippe cum amicitia pares semper aut accipiat aut faciat, sed ut arbiter et utrisque proximus aures darem et disceptantes duos medius segregarem.
thought_title: Caecilius's unease and the seating for the debate
orientation: The narrator Marcus is speaking; he and his friends have just watched boys playing on the shore, and now Caecilius shows distress at Octavius's earlier rebuke, so they sit down to debate.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, while all of us were being captivated by this pleasure of the spectacle, Caecilius was paying attention to nothing and was not laughing at the contest, but silent, anxious, standing apart, he was confessing by his face that he was grieved at something. To him I said: What is this matter? Why do I not recognize, Caecilius, that liveliness of yours? And I miss that cheerfulness of your eyes even in serious matters. Then he said: For a long time now the speech of our Octavius sharply torments and bites me, in which he attacked you and reproached you for negligence, so that he might accuse me, while pretending otherwise, more heavily of ignorance. Therefore I shall go further: I have a matter with Octavius about the whole and entire question. If it pleases, so that I, a man of his own sect, may dispute with him, he will now surely understand that it is easier to dispute among companions than to join wisdom together. Only let us sit down on these rocks thrown out for the protection of the baths and running out into the deep, so that we may both rest from the journey and dispute more intently. And with his word we sat down, in such a way that they protected me, the middle one of the three, by the surrounding of my side: and this was not an act of deference either of rank or of honor, since friendship always either receives or makes equals, but so that as judge and nearest to both I might give my ears and as the middle one separate the two disputants.

choices.english: a man of his own sect
choices.why: Caecilius identifies himself as belonging to the same philosophical or religious group as Octavius, setting up the debate as internal; 'sect' keeps the Latin term's sense of a school or faction.
The verb conserere means to entwine or join in close combat or discourse; rendering it literally preserves the metaphor of engaging wisdom in debate.

choices.english: thrown out for the protection of the baths
choices.why: The rocks are described as having been placed as a breakwater or protection for the baths; 'thrown out' keeps the literal sense of iactis.

choices.english: by the surrounding of my side
choices.why: The phrase describes the two friends flanking Marcus on either side; 'surrounding of my side' is literal and preserves the spatial image.
rejected: by the encircling of my flank

choices.why: Marcus is seated as the judge of the debate; 'judge' is the plain English equivalent and matches the brief's description of his role.

pass_b_english: So while all of us were carried away by the pleasure of the spectacle, Caecilius was paying no attention and not laughing at the contest. Silent, anxious, standing apart, his face confessed that something was troubling him.
I said to him, "What is this? Why do I not recognize that liveliness of yours, Caecilius? I miss that cheerfulness you used to have even in your eyes during serious matters."

Then he said, "For some time now the speech of our friend Octavius has been sharply tormenting and biting at me, the speech in which he attacked you and reproached you for negligence, so that by pretending to address you he was more severely accusing me of ignorance. So I will go further: my business with Octavius is total and complete. If it pleases you, as a man of the very sect he faults, let me debate with him, and he will soon understand that it is easier to debate among companions than to join wisdom together. Only let us sit down on those rocks thrown out for the protection of the baths and rising upward, so that we can both rest from the journey and debate more intently."

And with his words we sat down, so that, being the middle of the three, I might be protected by their desire. This was not out of deference to rank or honor, since friendship always makes or receives equals, but so that as judge and nearest to both I could give my ears to each and, seated in the middle, keep the two disputants apart.

problems.quote: by the surrounding of my side
problems.why: Latin says they protected me by ambition (their desire), not by "surrounding".
problems.fix: so that they might protect me, the middle of the three, by their desire

edits.old: so that the two of them protected me, the middle of the three, by the surrounding of my side.
edits.new: so that the two of them protected me, the middle of the three, by their desire.

fixed: Changed 'by the surrounding of my side' to 'by their desire' because the source 'ambitione protegerent' means they protected me by their desire, not by surrounding.

problems.quote: so that the two of them protected me, the middle of the three, by their desire.
problems.source_quote: ita ut me ex tribus medium lateris ambitione protegeret
problems.why: Latin says the middle party (the narrator) is protected by ambition, not that the two others protect him; agency reversed.
problems.fix: so that, being the middle of the three, I might be protected by their ambition.

edits.old: so that the two of them protected me, the middle of the three, by their desire.
edits.new: so that, being the middle of the three, I might be protected by their desire.

fixed: Corrected agency: source 'ita ut me ex tribus medium lateris ambitione protegeret' means the narrator as middle one is protected by their desire, not that the two protect him.

problems.source_quote: et in altum procurrentibus petrarum obicibus
problems.why: Latin describes stones that rise upward, not a deep running.
problems.ruling: Latin 'in altum procurrentibus' = jutting out high/upward (of rocks), not 'running out into the deep' (water).

fixed: Changed 'running out into the deep' to 'rising upward': source 'in altum procurrentibus' means the rocks extend upward, not into deep water.

fixed.quote: since I am a man of his own sect
fixed.fix: as a man of the very sect he faults
fixed.note: Caecilius is a pagan, so 'his own sect' wrongly makes him share Octavius's faith; ipsius most likely means the very sect Octavius criticized.

polish.changed: Clarified that Caecilius is the one speaking in the third paragraph, made the narrator's role as judge explicit, and smoothed the sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: Minucius Felix (fl. c. 200) was a Roman lawyer and Christian apologist
notes.why: The narrator is named Marcus in the text but introduced only as 'the author' and 'Minucius Felix' in the intro, which may confuse readers about who is speaking.
notes.fix: Clarify that Marcus is Minucius Felix.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Octavius suddenly calls Caecilius 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks it's a new person.
notes.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.
